title: Filtering, Sorting & Grouping Data with SELECT/WHERE/HAVING
summary: Master SQL's true logical evaluation order (`FROM -> WHERE -> GROUP BY -> HAVING -> SELECT -> ORDER BY -> LIMIT`) and three-valued NULL traps.
learningObjectives: Filter raw rows efficiently before aggregation using WHERE and aggregate groups cleanly via HAVING
Handle NULLs reliably using IS NULL, COALESCE(), and three-valued logic

sections.heading: 1. True Logical Execution Order & NULL Traps
sections.content:
Although you write `SELECT` first, SQL evaluates clauses in a strict pipeline: **1. FROM/JOIN -> 2. WHERE -> 3. GROUP BY -> 4. HAVING -> 5. SELECT (computing aliases!) -> 6. ORDER BY -> 7. LIMIT**. Knowing this explains instantly why you CANNOT reference a `SELECT` alias inside `WHERE`, and why `WHERE` runs BEFORE grouping while `HAVING` runs AFTER!

Watch out for SQL's three-valued logic (`TRUE`, `FALSE`, `UNKNOWN`): comparing `email != 'bob@x.com'` on a `NULL` row yields `UNKNOWN`, silently dropping NULL rows unless you write `WHERE email IS DISTINCT FROM 'bob@x.com'` or explicit `IS NULL`!

codeExamples.code:
[FROM / JOIN] --> [WHERE row filters] --> [GROUP BY buckets] --> [HAVING group filters]
                                                                        |
[LIMIT / OFFSET] <-- [ORDER BY] <-- [SELECT expressions & aliases] <-----+
codeExamples.explanation: SQL builds rows, removes filtered entries early via WHERE, summarizes buckets, then projects SELECT columns.

keyPoints: Filter early in `WHERE` (not `HAVING`) whenever conditions apply to non-aggregated rows—letting indexes eliminate unnecessary grouping work!
Always test NULL edge cases explicitly (`IS NULL`, `COALESCE(val, 0)`).
commonMistakes: Checking `WHERE deleted_at = NULL` (which always returns 0 rows!) instead of `WHERE deleted_at IS NULL`.

sections.heading: 2. Grouped Revenue & Retention Reporting Query
sections.content: Look how cleanly `WHERE`, `GROUP BY`, `HAVING`, and `COALESCE` synthesize raw event logs into actionable management analytics.

codeExamples.code:
SELECT
  d.department_name,
  COUNT(e.id) AS active_headcount,
  ROUND(AVG(COALESCE(e.salary, 0)), 2) AS avg_compensation
FROM departments d
INNER JOIN employees e ON d.id = e.department_id
WHERE e.terminated_at IS NULL
GROUP BY d.id, d.department_name
HAVING COUNT(e.id) >= 5
ORDER BY avg_compensation DESC;
codeExamples.explanation: Filtering `terminated_at IS NULL` in WHERE skips terminated staff before grouping, while `HAVING COUNT >= 5` drops tiny teams safely.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: Departments with >= 5 active staff sorted cleanly from highest average pay downward

keyPoints: Use `COUNT(*)` for row counts and `COUNT(col)` only when counting strictly non-null column values.
commonMistakes: Putting non-aggregated columns inside `SELECT` without listing them cleanly in `GROUP BY`.

exercises.title: Analyze Cohort Grades With Filtering & NULL Handling
exercises.objective: Author a deterministic grouped query distinguishing row filters vs aggregate thresholds.
exercises.description: From `submissions(id, cohort_name, score, graded_at)`, list cohorts averaging `>= 80` across graded rows (`graded_at IS NOT NULL`) with at least 10 submissions.
instructions: Filter strictly ungraded pending rows out in `WHERE` (`graded_at IS NOT NULL`).
Group by `cohort_name` calculating count and rounded average score.
Filter cohorts using `HAVING` matching both count `>= 10` and `AVG(score) >= 80`.
exercises.starterCode:
SELECT cohort_name, COUNT(*) AS total, ROUND(AVG(score), 1) AS avg_score
FROM submissions
-- Add WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY
hints: Un-graded NULL scores must be skipped before AVG runs using `WHERE graded_at IS NOT NULL`.
exercises.submissionRequirements: Complete all checklist items, test assumptions, and document verification rationale.
evaluationCriteria: Addresses the root architectural/technical challenge accurately
Follows defensive industry standards and edge-case validation
exercises.solutionExplanation: Filtering `graded_at IS NOT NULL` first avoids diluting or ignoring rows improperly before computing `HAVING COUNT(*) >= 10 AND AVG(score) >= 80`.

knowledgeChecks.prompt: Why does `SELECT * FROM tasks WHERE completed_at = NULL` return ZERO rows even when NULL rows exist?

options.text: In SQL three-valued logic, `= NULL` evaluates to `UNKNOWN` rather than `TRUE`; you must write `IS NULL`
PostgreSQL hides NULL rows by default
The `=` operator works only on integers

knowledgeChecks.explanation: SQL requires `IS NULL` / `IS NOT NULL` because NULL denotes missing unknown state, not equality.

knowledgeChecks.prompt: If you can filter active records using either `WHERE active = true` or putting `active = true` inside `HAVING`, which performs far better on large tables?

options.text: `WHERE` runs before grouping and can utilize B-Tree indexes directly, cutting memory and aggregation cost
They execute identical plans regardless of size
SQL ignores `WHERE` when `GROUP BY` is present

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Push row-level filters into WHERE early to shrink intermediate rows prior to aggregation.

knowledgeChecks.prompt: What will `COUNT(*)` vs `COUNT(phone)` return on a 10-row users table where 3 users have NULL phone numbers?

recap: You mastered SQL clause execution order, three-valued NULL handling, and accurate WHERE vs HAVING filtering.
